_ext: keys below are pipeline extensions, additive to SPEC SS4
protagonist: Grace Liu, cabinet shop production manager

deliverables.text: A cut-list conversion table: for every stile/rail width on Appendix A's cut list, show the width written both as a mixed number and as an improper fraction, converting explicitly in both directions -- the mill's order form and the shop's rip-saw gauge use these two forms interchangeably, and a mismatch between them is how the wrong stock gets ordered.

A rough-width calculation for Standard Stock, shown step by step in fraction form only (no decimals): starting from the 7/4" net finished width, add Appendix B's jointing allowance and saw-kerf allowance using a common denominator, then convert the resulting improper fraction back into a mixed number -- this is the actual rough width Grace must buy per stile.

A waste-log reconciliation: using Appendix D's rip-crew logs, simplify every unsimplified fraction entry and show, with the arithmetic, which logged entries describe the exact same physical waste width and which (if any) genuinely differ -- before any total waste figure may be trusted, every entry must be reduced to lowest terms and compared fairly.

A true cost-per-door comparison, computed entirely in fraction/mixed-number arithmetic: Standard Stock's cost (Appendix B's price per board foot applied to D2's true rough width, including waste) against The Special Order's cost (Appendix C's exact-width price, applied only above its stated minimum board footage) -- and the batch size, in number of doors, at which The Special Order's total cost per door first drops below Standard Stock's.

An original visual display (a scaled fraction bar or strip diagram, in eighths) showing, for one stile, how much of Standard Stock's rough width becomes net finished stock and how much becomes waste, set beside The Special Order's exact-width strip with no waste -- built from the D2 and D4 figures.

appendices.title: Standard Stock: Milling Allowances and Price (Option A)

balance.argument_a: Standard Stock's argument is availability and control: no minimum order, no lead time, and the shop already owns the equipment -- but its true cost is not the sticker width. Every stile/rail requires a rough width of 7/4 in (net) + 1/4 in (jointing allowance [S1]) + 1/8 in (kerf allowance [S2]) = 17/8 in (2-1/8 in), found by converting to a common denominator (eighths) before adding. Over this job's 96 pieces (24 doors x 4 pieces/door, each 2 ft long), that comes to 34 board feet at $8.99/board foot [S3] = $305.66 total, or $12.7358.../door -- a real, recurring cost from width that becomes sawdust and jointer waste on every single piece, not a rounding error.
balance.argument_b: The Special Order's argument is zero width waste: the mill supplies the exact 7/4 in width, so no jointing or kerf allowance is ever paid for. At $9.34/board foot [S3, S4] the job's exact need is 28 board feet, but Appendix E's 30-board-foot minimum (MA1) means Grace must buy 30 board feet regardless, for a total of $280.20, or $11.675/door -- genuinely cheaper than Standard Stock's $12.7358.../door, a real 8.33% margin. The case for B is fragile at smaller batch sizes: the breakeven batch size is 23 doors (below that, the unused minimum-order footage outweighs B's per-board-foot savings) -- this job's 24 doors clears that threshold by exactly one door, not by a comfortable margin.
balance.margin_basis: margin = |cost_per_door(A) - cost_per_door(B)| / max(cost_per_door(A), cost_per_door(B)) at this job's batch size of 24 doors. cost_per_door(A) = (96 pieces x 17/8 in width x 24 in length x 1 in thickness / 144) x $8.99 / 24 doors = 34 bd ft x $8.99 / 24 = $12.7358.../door (constant regardless of batch size -- Standard Stock has no minimum). cost_per_door(B) = max(30 bd ft [MA1], 28 bd ft needed) x $9.34 / 24 doors = 30 x $9.34 / 24 = $11.675/door. margin = |12.7358 - 11.675| / 12.7358 = 8.33%. Within the project's 5-10% target band. Breakeven batch size (smallest integer n where cost_per_door(B,n) < cost_per_door(A)): for n <= 25, B must still buy the full 30-bd-ft minimum, so cost_per_door(B,n) = 30 x 9.34 / n, which first drops below $12.7358 at n=23 (280.2/23 = $12.18 < $12.7358; at n=22, 280.2/22 = $12.7364, still fractionally above A). This job's batch of 24 doors clears the 23-door threshold by exactly one door.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Minimum order quantity (board feet) the mill requires to run a custom exact-width dimensioning job
modeling_assumptions.basis: No source publishes a minimum-order figure specific to a small custom exact-width dimensioning run. Real reported/published minimums for adjacent custom-milling services range from 'no minimum -- order one board' (Estate Millwork, cut-to-size individual boards) to a 100-board-foot minimum reported for custom log sawing (WoodWeb trade forum) to a 500-board-foot minimum for bulk wholesale hardwood (Estate Millwork's wholesale terms). 30 board feet is chosen near the low end of this real range, appropriate for a small-shop custom width-dimensioning run (a narrower, more specialized service than either extreme).
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: This is the case's single load-bearing, dilemma-relevant dial. Under the current 30-board-foot value, The Special Order (B) is the cheaper option for this job's 24-door batch by a real 8.33% margin, and the breakeven batch size is 23 doors -- this job clears that threshold by exactly one door. A Hero who argues the real minimum should be somewhat higher would push the breakeven batch size up and could flip the recommendation to A for this exact job size; a Hero arguing it should be lower would make B's advantage more comfortable. Work the D4 comparison yourself with a different assumed minimum rather than taking 30 board feet as unchallengeable fact.

sensitivity_note: No illness, death, or severe hardship; ordinary small-business schedule/budget pressure on a fixed-bid job with a client-facing deadline. SPEC SS6 one-line flag not required beyond noting the deadline stress for the discussion lead.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: No mill publishes a minimum-order-quantity figure for this exact scenario (a small custom exact-width dimensioning run) -- 30 board feet is a constructed, disclosed Modeling Assumption (MA1), not a measurable present fact about a specific real mill. context_glossary.desc: The vertical frame member of a cabinet door -- paired with horizontal rails, stiles form the door's outer frame around its center panel.
The frame pieces of a cabinet door: stiles are the vertical members, rails are the horizontal ones -- together they form the door's frame around its center panel.
A unit of lumber volume equal to a piece 12 in x 12 in x 1 in -- the standard unit hardwood is priced and sold by, no matter the board's actual length or width.
A unit of lumber volume equal to a piece 12 in x 12 in x 1 in -- the standard unit hardwood is priced and sold by, no matter the board's actual length or width.
The width of material a saw blade actually removes as it cuts -- that narrow slice becomes sawdust, not usable stock.
A saw cut made lengthwise, parallel to the wood grain, to reduce a board's width -- different from a crosscut, which cuts across the grain.
To shave thin layers off a board's surface with a hand plane or powered planer, smoothing it or bringing it down to a target thickness.
The width machined off one edge of a rough board by a jointer to make that edge perfectly flat and straight before it is safely ripped to width.
Had one edge machined flat and straight by a jointer, so the board has a true, straight reference edge before it is safely ripped to width.

"Surfaced four sides" -- lumber machined smooth and square on all four faces at the mill, ready to use without further milling. That's a step up from S1S and S2S ("surfaced one side" / "surfaced two sides"), lighter grades hardwood suppliers also sell that are planed smooth on only one or two faces, leaving the rest rough and requiring more milling before use.
A large stationary saw -- mounted vertically or horizontally -- built to break full sheets of plywood, MDF, or other sheet goods down into smaller, sized pieces.

A board's named, advertised size (e.g. a "1 inch" board) is bigger than its actual finished size after milling and drying -- the real, usable dimension is always somewhat smaller than the nominal one.
A contract where the price is agreed in advance and does not change no matter how much the job actually ends up costing the contractor to complete.

A lumber-processing business with its own saws and planing equipment -- a shop can either buy standard stock off the shelf or send (or place an order with) a mill to have wood custom-cut to an exact width or thickness it doesn't stock.
A shop document listing every piece a job needs -- exact dimensions, quantities, and material -- so a carpenter cuts to a plan instead of re-deriving sizes at the bench each time.

The packaging a replacement saw blade ships in -- like a spec sheet, it states the blade's own measurements (diameter, kerf width, arbor size) in fractions of an inch, the same convention this trade uses everywhere else.

catalog.ask: Two ways to buy the same hardwood: mill it in-house with no minimum order, or special-order it pre-cut with a required 30-board-foot minimum. Grace's shop has argued about which is smarter for years -- nobody's actually run the numbers on a single door.
